newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weak yen, sales tax rise spark Japan price worries.
newsitem.headline: Weak yen, sales tax rise spark Japan price worries.

text.p: Alarm is growing among Japan's monetary authorities over rising prices after the sales tax increase on April 1 and steeper import bills reflecting the yen's fall against the dollar.
Officials say there are no fears of inflation in Japan at the moment, but that future price movements need to be carefully watched.
An official at Economic Planning Agency's (EPA) price research division said on Friday only a limited number of goods so far reflect a rise in import costs.
But he said: "Upward pressure on prices must have increased by now as the dollar has risen further above 120 yen."
The EPA said last November that upward pressure on import prices from a weakening yen had been cushioned by severe competition and Japanese consumers' preference for cheaper goods.

Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita said on Sunday that the central bank will look at how recent weakness of the yen against the dollar and an improving supply/demand balance might affect prices of goods in Japan.
In a quarterly economic outlook released on April 25, the BOJ said prices in Japan have stopped declining and attention to exchange rates was required in regard to prices.

Consumer price data issued on the same day showed a 1.2 percent rise for the Tokyo area in April from a year earlier. It was the biggest rise since March 1994 and followed the April 1 increase in the sales tax to five percent from three percent.
Japan's April wholesale price data is released on May 9 and the nationwide consumer price data for April on May 30.

"We had expected that the sales tax rise might boost nationwide consumer prices by 1.5 percent when it is completely added to prices. But the Tokyo data showed prices have not risen much so far," the EPA official said.

But prices of some imported goods in the Tokyo area showed a significant increase, the official said. Imported beef prices, for example, rose 9.5 percent in April from a year earlier. Prices of imported golf clubs rose 5.7 percent year-on-year and imported passenger cars rose 2.8 percent.

"The speed of import price rises was still moderate compared to that of the yen's fall against the dollar," he said. The dollar has risen more than 15 percent from around 107 yen a year ago. It rose as high as 127.47 yen on Thursday, its highest level since August 1992.
Given monetary authorities' worries over inflation, falls in yields of long-term Japanese government bonds (JGBs) may be curbed, economists and traders said.

"The market is not so worried about prices. But it is clear that the BOJ governor has started to talk about prices as an alibi before a credit tightening," said a senior dealer at a "Big Four" brokerage.

Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities Japan, said the weak yen had gradually affected import prices from late 1996. But overall prices failed to reflect the upward pressure because they were offset by price falls in industrial goods.
Kato said, however, that wholesale prices may rise by more than the margin of the sales tax increase by mid-1997 and consumer price rises may then get closer to two percent.

"It seems the market has already priced in tight supply, a major driving force of the recent rally. The rebound in 10-year JGB yields, which had fallen below 2.3 percent at one stage, suggested a shift in the market's focus to economic fundamentals from the supply/demand balance," Kato said.

Steady buying by investors, including Japanese insurers and public funds, had fuelled a rally in JGBs since earlier this year and the yield of the 2.6 percent 193rd JGB due March 2007 equalled its life-low of 2.245 percent on April 8.
The bond yield stood at 2.480 percent in late Friday trade. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-33432-8570
